newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to unveil plan to stretch debt maturity.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to unveil plan to stretch debt maturity.

text.p: Pakistan's new government, facing a debt payment crunch, hopes to reduce its short-term liabilities by borrowing up to $1 billion long term from expatriate Pakistanis, analysts said on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who took office on Monday after winning February 3 elections, has appealed to Pakistanis abroad to remit deposits of $1,000 each to bolster foreign reserves.

"Although this seems to be a stop-gap measure, it is essentially necessary to allow the government and the economy to gain some breathing space," Kalim Aziz, research head at ING Baring Securities brokerage house, told Reuters.
"With a potential extension of debt maturity from six months to two years, Pakistan has a better chance of meeting forex-related liabilities," he added.

ING Baring Securities said in a report that the government hoped to raise at least $1 billion from the appeal, which it said bankers had discussed at a recent meeting with State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) governor Muhammad Yaqub.
Pakistan's foreign debt stood at $28.6 billion at the end of fiscal 1995/96 (July-June), up from $27.1 billion in 1994/95.
External debt accounted for 44.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1995/96, 52.2 percent of export earnings and 33.9 percent of total foreign exchange earnings, SBP figures show.
Analysts say the ratio of foreign debt servicing to foreign exchange earnings will be well over 30 percent in 1996/97.
The ING Baring report said the scheme would offer investors two percent above LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate) for one-year deposits in dollars, sterling or Deutsche marks.
It said the maximum rate of return for five-year dollar deposits would be nine percent a year, 9.75 percent for sterling deposits and seven percent for Deutsche mark deposits.
"The Ministry of Finance is also in the process of launching a domestic rupee-based deposit scheme with attractive rates of return to mobilise funds to retire the domestic debt," it said.
Pakistan's outstanding domestic debt amounted to a provisional 908.9 billion rupees ($22.6 billion) at the end of 1995/96, up from 798.6 billion a year earlier, the SBP said.
Interest payments on domestic debt equalled 33.5 percent of total tax revenue, 27.4 percent of total revenue, 24.5 percent of current spending and 20 percent of total spending, it said.
"We expect the government to be able to raise a significant amount from these two schemes, which will help in managing its immediate balance of payments problems," the report said.

The International Monetary Fund's executive director for Pakistan, Abbas Mirakhor, was scheduled to arrive on Wednesday for talks expected to focus on looming debt payments and targets agreed to by the IMF with the departing caretaker government.

Foreign bankers say Mirakhor might ask the new government how it plans to meet debt repayments of an estimated $200 million due this month and $587 million due in March with liquid foreign reserves now at only $796 million.
They say the IMF might express concern at more than $1 billion in costly short-term borrowing by the caretaker government during its 90 days in office from November 5.
